world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kuot is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword item, Lindström & Remijsen 2005 (Linguistics 43(4): 839-870), is squarely about Kuot word stress and intonation; only its abstract could be read (OpenAlex), which states that word stress is lexically determined, duration-cued, with no F0 correlate. The full text is closed access with no repository copy, and every open route tried by automated download (De Gruyter/degruyterbrill landing and PDF: HTTP 202 empty; Edinburgh Research Explorer: an automated-access block/404; Remijsen's archived homepage: citation only, no PDF; DiVA: connection refused; scholar.archive. BASE: bot-gated; the Internet Archive's index: offline; The best first-hand stress statement actually read is Lindström's 2002 thesis, section 3.5 Stress (pp. 112-117; the chapter PDF and text were already held by the project from an earlier reading and were read in full): stress is lexical, must be known per lexeme, realised chiefly as duration and not pitch, with minimal pairs and occasional grammatical stress shift. New records saved: OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar metadata JSONs and the 2020 Internet Archive copy of Remijsen's Edinburgh publication list, all logged in Since there is no catalog record, supersedes_catalog_source is false; the thesis section would be the deciding source for a new Kuot entry (lexical stress), with the 2005 paper as the stronger phonetic confirmation once obtained.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress position is a lexical property of each lexeme; there is no syllable- or mora-based rule. It is cued by duration (with some intensity), not by pitch, which is used for clause intonation. Minimal pairs: ŋa'ne 'meat/vegetable accompaniment' vs 'ŋane 'strong-3m'; ka'ranim 'reef, low tide; year' vs 'baranim 'store; bird net'. Chapter opening (p. 85): 'Stress is not predictable from general principles (i.e., it is lexical), and is manifested primarily as duration.' Summary (p. 117): 'pitch is used primarily for intonation.. while word stress is achieved primarily through duration.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Author notes a possible 'combination of two stressed syllables' in a word when a stem with inherent stress carries a stress-attracting enclitic (duk 'thunder' + subject enclitic), but treats interactions as beyond scope (p. 117).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift is occasionally an exponent of a grammatical category: future of some class II verbs, e.g. i-abǝ ['jabǝ] 'she climbs' vs i-aba [ja'ba] 'she will climb' (ex. 88, p. 117). Some grammatical morphemes often but not always attract stress, notably the non-singular suffix -(i)p on nouns and the subject enclitics of verb class I. Possible inherent stress distinguishing homophone pairs duk 'break/thunder', ut 'be full/be like'. Footnote 13 (p. 112): stress is not marked on Kuot forms in the thesis because the author distrusted her early transcriptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word (lexeme) level stress within the grammatical word; demonstrated on words in utterance-final, sentence-medial and topicalised-phrase positions with instrumental figures (Figs 2-5b, pp. 113-116); pitch belongs to clause-level intonation (§3.6). Analysis explicitly labelled 'preliminary'.
new_statements.identity_note: Lindström's description is based on fieldwork in Bimun village (west coast, southern Kuot area); she notes that Panaras (northern) speakers regard their dialect as more original and that the SIL Chungs worked at Kabil on the east coast. No dialect glottocodes under kuot1243 were seen; the statement is taken as language-level for kuot1243.

new_statements.citation: Lindström, Eva. 2002. Topics in the grammar of Kuot, a non-Austronesian language of New Ireland, Papua New Guinea. PhD dissertation, Department of Linguistics, Stockholm University (ISBN 91-7265-459-7). Chapter 3 Phonology, section 3.5 Stress, pp. 112-117.
new_statements.locator: Section 3.5 Stress, opening paragraphs, p. 112; summary sentence p. 117 ("In summary, pitch is used primarily for intonation.., while word stress is achieved primarily through duration.")
new_statements.reading: Kuot has lexical (unpredictable) word stress: no syllable- or mora-based rule, position must be listed per lexeme, with minimal pairs such as ŋa'ne 'meat/vegetable side dish' vs 'ŋane 'strong-3m' and ka'ranim 'reef, low tide; year' vs 'baranim 'store; bird net' (pp. 113-116). Stress is cued chiefly by duration (plus some intensity), not by pitch, which carries clause-level intonation. Some grammatical morphemes (non-singular -(i)p, class I subject enclitics) often but not always attract stress, and stress shift marks the future in some class II verbs (i-abǝ ['jabǝ] 'she climbs' vs i-aba [ja'ba] 'she will climb', p. 117). The author warns that stress was hard for her to perceive and is therefore not marked on most cited forms (fn. 13, p. 112). For catalog purposes: lexical/unpredictable stress; no fixed-position coding applies.

sources.locator: Ch. 3 Phonology, §3.5 'Stress', p. 112 (PDF page 28 of the chapter file); summary sentence p. 117; chapter overview p. 85
sources.note: Stress is lexical (position must be known per lexeme; no rules referring to syllables or moras), realised chiefly by duration (and some intensity), not pitch; pitch is reserved for clause intonation; some endings attract stress; stress shift marks future in some class II verbs; minimal pairs ŋa'ne vs 'ŋane, ka'ranim vs 'baranim shown instrumentally; author omits stress marks in the thesis because she did not trust her early transcriptions.

sources.quote: Word stress, on the other hand, does not interact with intonation in terms of its encoding. It displays a very stable correlation with duration but no association with F 0 ; in other words, there is no consistent marking of stress by means of F 0 in Kuot. The position of Kuot word stress is lexically determined, yielding minimal stress pairs. [...] A phonetic analysis of minimal stress pairs recorded in controlled environments demonstrates that lexically stressed syllables do not correlate with pitch.
